analysis.one_liner: Extends minimum wage and overtime protections to most home care workers and funds workforce data collection.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 35 Democratic cosponsors, never got a committee hearing or a floor vote and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would end the exemption that lets home care and companionship workers be paid below minimum wage with no overtime pay, while keeping the exemption only for truly casual help like a family friend who visits a few hours a week. It would also require states to report annually on whether they have enough direct care workers, and it would fund grants to recruit, train, and retain these workers. Around 10 million elderly and disabled Americans rely on this workforce, and the bill's own findings say nearly half of the workers live in households receiving public benefits like food stamps.
analysis.who_benefits: Direct care workers — home health aides, personal care aides, and nursing assistants — who would gain federal minimum wage and overtime protections and access to state-funded training, wage, and retention grants. The 10 million elderly and disabled Americans who depend on them would benefit indirectly from a more stable workforce.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Home care aides and the elderly people they serve

how_it_helps.text: Narrows the Fair Labor Standards Act exemption so that only genuinely casual companionship workers stay exempt from minimum wage and overtime rules; workers employed by an agency, or working more than 5 hours a week or 12 weeks a year for a household, would be covered.
Requires every state Medicaid program to report annually to HHS on the size, wages, turnover, and vacancies of its direct care workforce, including states operating under waivers.

Directs HHS to award competitive three-year grants to states and other entities to improve recruitment, retention, and education of direct care workers, including initiatives that raise wages and benefits and build career ladders.
Funds state and tribal data collection systems and requires the National Health Care Workforce Commission to report annually on direct care workforce supply and demand.

analysis.who_pays: Home care agencies and long-term care providers would bear higher labor costs from wage and overtime coverage. State Medicaid programs would bear new reporting obligations and potentially higher program costs. Families paying out of pocket for in-home help would face higher prices in some cases.
analysis.who_pays_short: Home care agencies and Medicaid programs

drawbacks.text: Extending wage and overtime coverage to agency-employed home care workers raises the cost of paid long-term care, which families paying privately and state Medicaid budgets would partially absorb; some agencies could respond by cutting hours or services.
The bill carries no dedicated appropriation: the grant programs are authorized at 'such sums as may be necessary,' so the promised workforce investments would still depend on later spending bills.
Its data collection and monitoring provisions require administrative work from state Medicaid agencies without adding funding for them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core wage-and-overtime change targets a workforce the bill's own findings describe as earning about $17,000 a year on average, with 45% living at or below the poverty level. The main cost — higher labor prices passed to families and Medicaid — is real but moderate, and the bill preserves the exemption for genuinely casual help. On balance, a focused, low-cost bill for a low-paid workforce, though it was light on dedicated funding.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Energy and Commerce and Education and the Workforce committees, then to subcommittees, and neither committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Linda Sánchez introduced the bill on June 23, 2011, with 35 cosponsors, all Democrats.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Education and the Workforce committees, then to the Subcommittee on Health and the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections.
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — is recorded before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Home care agencies kept the exemption allowing below-minimum pay for their workers, and no provider bore the added wage costs. The roughly 2 million direct care workers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Home care agencies; workers gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Linda Sánchez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through referral.

for.name: 35 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 35 were Democrats.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill in its Health Subcommittee and never took further action.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill in its Workforce Protections Subcommittee and never took further action.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor or scheduled committee action during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 35 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the House majority in the 112th Congress was Republican, and the bill never reached the floor.

industries.industry: Home care and home health agencies
industries.note: The bill would remove these agencies' access to the exemption that allows paying agency-employed home care workers below minimum wage with no overtime, raising their labor costs. Their interest in keeping the exemption runs against the workers' wages, which the bill's findings say often leave nearly half of the workforce on public benefits.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and long-term care facilities
industries.note: Many of their direct care employees are covered by wage law already, but the bill's Medicaid reporting requirements and workforce grants would touch the whole sector; its reporting and monitoring provisions add compliance work while its retention grants could help with chronic staffing shortages.

States would face new annual workforce reporting duties without dedicated funding, but would also be eligible for data collection and recruitment grants, and a more stable workforce could reduce state spending on turnover-related problems.
